question.text: A debt AIF holds a corporate bond with coupon 9% paid semi-annually. The last coupon was 3 months ago. When reporting fair value of the bond to investors, the 'dirty price' includes:

answer.text: Only the present value of future coupons (clean price only)
The clean price PLUS accrued interest (since last coupon date to valuation date)
The face value plus the next coupon, ignoring time value
Only the sale price in the latest exchange trade

explanation.text: The Logic: In fixed-income mathematics, the "clean price" is the present value of the bond's future coupon and principal cash flows, while the "dirty price" (also called the invoice price) adds the accrued interest from the last coupon date to the valuation/settlement date. For a 9% semi-annual coupon bond three months after the last coupon, accrued interest is roughly (9%/2) x (3/6) = 2.25% of par. For NAV reporting, dirty price is appropriate because the bond's full economic value to the fund includes the accrued coupon that has been earned but not yet paid. The Trap: Clean-price-only (A) ignores accrued interest and understates the fund's economic claim. Face value plus next coupon ignoring time value (C) abandons present-value mathematics. Latest exchange trade only (D) ignores any accrual that has occurred since the trade. Note: The specific "dirty price = clean price + accrued interest" terminology is not used in the cited workbook chapter (FINAL_Series-XIX-C_AIF Managers_Ver-Dec-2025.pdf, pp. 242, 368-369, 392-393), which discusses the fixed-income PV formula and Cat III amortized-cost-plus-accrued-interest valuation for unlisted securities. The framing above is general fixed-income/industry knowledge.
